Reading R's own object header

Source: vignettes/articles/sexp-header.Rmd
sexp-header.Rmd

Every R object lives in memory behind a fixed-size C header, the SEXPREC: a word of bitfields, three pointers and, for a vector, its length. A fixed-size record is exactly what bin_layout() describes, so the header makes a small worked example of a layout over bytes that zubin did not write: native byte order, a bitfield word, pointers, and a body at a known offset.

This is a way to look, not a way to program. The structure is private to R (it is in R’s Defn.h, not in its API), it changes between R versions, and nothing here belongs in a package. To inspect an object in earnest use lobstr::sxp(), or .Internal(inspect(x)) at the console; the last section says how each reads the header. The page assumes a 64-bit build of R 4.x, where the header is 48 bytes.

Getting the bytes

zubin reads raw vectors, and no R function hands over an object’s own memory, so the page compiles a three-line C function that copies the first n bytes of the header into one:

stopifnot(.Machine$sizeof.pointer == 8)
library(zubin)

src <- tempfile(fileext = ".c")
writeLines(c(
  "#include <string.h>",
  "#include <Rinternals.h>",
  "SEXP peek(SEXP x, SEXP n) {",
  "  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(RAWSXP, Rf_asInteger(n)));",
  "  memcpy(RAW(out), (const void *) x, (size_t) XLENGTH(out));",
  "  UNPROTECT(1);",
  "  return out;",
  "}"
), src)
system2(file.path(R.home("bin"), "R"), c("CMD", "SHLIB", shQuote(src)), stdout = FALSE)
dll <- dyn.load(sub("\\.c$", .Platform$dynlib.ext, src))
peek <- function(x, n = 48L) .Call(dll$peek, x, n)

peek() copies as many bytes as it is asked for, and nothing checks them against the object: the caller asks for no more than the object holds. An integer vector of three elements holds 48 bytes of header and 12 of data.

x <- c(10L, 20L, 30L)
b <- peek(x, 60L)
bin_hexdump(b)
#> 00000000: 0d00 0040 0300 0000 208f cb23 b355 0000  ...@.... ..#.U..
#> 00000010: c841 1b28 b355 0000 4842 1b28 b355 0000  .A.(.U..HB.(.U..
#> 00000020: 0300 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000  ................
#> 00000030: 0a00 0000 1400 0000 1e00 0000            ............

The layout

On a 64-bit build the header is:

Offset Field C type
0 sxpinfo 64 bits of bitfields
8 attrib SEXP, the attribute pairlist
16 gengc_next_node SEXP, the garbage collector’s list
24 gengc_prev_node SEXP
32 length R_xlen_t, vectors only
40 truelength R_xlen_t, vectors only
48 the data what INTEGER(x), REAL(x) and the rest point to

This is memory of the running process, so the byte order is the host’s: =, never a guess at little-endian. sxpinfo is two u32 because a u64 that holds bitfields can pass 2^53, past what a double holds exactly; the pointers are user-space addresses, far below 2^53, and read as b8 to be printed in hexadecimal. next is a reserved word in R, so the pointer fields take other names.

header <- bin_layout(
  "= info:u32[2] attrib:b8 gc_next:b8 gc_prev:b8 length:i64 truelength:i64"
)
header
#> <zubin_layout: 48 bytes, 6 fields>
#>  name       type count size offset endian
#>  info       u32  2     8     0     little
#>  attrib     b8   1     8     8           
#>  gc_next    b8   1     8    16           
#>  gc_prev    b8   1     8    24           
#>  length     i64  1     8    32     little
#>  truelength i64  1     8    40     little
h <- bin_unpack(b, header)
h[c("length", "truelength")]
#>   length truelength
#> 1      3          0
bin_decode(b, "i32", offset = 48, n = h$length, endian = "native")
#> [1] 10 20 30

The bitfields

zubin has no bitfield type: a field is whole bytes. The bits come out with arithmetic on the two words. GCC and Clang allocate bitfields from the least significant bit on the targets R runs on, which gives, in R 4.x:

Word Bits Field
1 0–4 type, the SEXPTYPE (13 is INTSXP)
1 5, 6, 7 scalar, obj (has a class), alt (ALTREP)
1 8–23 gp, general-purpose bits
1 24–27 mark, debug, trace, spare
1 28, 29–31 gcgen, gccls (the collector’s generation and size class)
2 0–15 named, the reference count
2 16–31 extra 
bits <- function(v, from, width) (v %/% 2^from) %% 2^width

sxpinfo <- function(h) {
  w1 <- h$info.1
  w2 <- h$info.2
  data.frame(
    type = bits(w1, 0, 5), scalar = bits(w1, 5, 1), obj = bits(w1, 6, 1),
    alt = bits(w1, 7, 1), gp = bits(w1, 8, 16), gcgen = bits(w1, 28, 1),
    gccls = bits(w1, 29, 3), named = bits(w2, 0, 16)
  )
}

address <- function(p) paste0("0x", sub("^0+", "", paste(rev(as.character(p)), collapse = "")))

sxpinfo(h)
#>   type scalar obj alt gp gcgen gccls named
#> 1   13      0   0   0  0     0     2     3

What the header shows

A second binding to the same vector raises its reference count, and copies nothing:

refs <- function(x) sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(x), header))$named
before <- refs(x)
y <- x
c(before = before, after = refs(x))
#> before  after 
#>      4      6

Without attributes, attrib points to NULL, which is one object of its own, so every bare object points to the same address. An attribute makes it a pairlist of its own:

attrib <- function(x) address(bin_unpack(peek(x), header)$attrib[[1]])
z <- structure(c(1, 2), units = "cm")
c(double = attrib(c(1, 2)), string = attrib("a"), with_attr = attrib(z))
#>           double           string        with_attr 
#> "0x55b323cb8f20" "0x55b323cb8f20" "0x55b329b81b60"

1:3 is an ALTREP object, a compact sequence that stores its start and end, not its elements: alt is set, and the 16 bytes at offset 32 hold ALTREP’s own pointers, not a length.

sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(1:3), header))[c("type", "alt")]
#>   type alt
#> 1   13   1

A class sets obj:

sxpinfo(bin_unpack(peek(factor("a")), header))[c("type", "obj")]
#>   type obj
#> 1   13   1

The same fields, as R prints them; the ATTRIB address is the one attrib() read above:

.Internal(inspect(z))
#> @55b329b43308 14 REALSXP g0c2 [REF(2),ATT] (len=2, tl=0) 1,2
#> ATTRIB:
#>   @55b329b81b60 02 LISTSXP g0c0 [REF(1)] 
#>     TAG: @55b323dc6f48 01 SYMSXP g1c0 [MARK,REF(155),LCK,gp=0x4000] "units" (has value)
#>     @55b329b18c88 16 STRSXP g0c1 [REF(6)] (len=1, tl=0)
#>       @55b32447b848 09 CHARSXP g1c1 [MARK,REF(97),gp=0x61] [ASCII] [cached] "cm"

How the real tools read the header

peek() is one of three ways to see these fields, and the only one that can break without warning.

  • .Internal(inspect(x)) is part of R. It is compiled from R’s own sources against the private Defn.h, in the same build as the structure it prints, so it can read every bit and never falls out of step with the layout. Its output format is not promised, and .Internal() is for R’s own code: use it at the console, never in a package.
  • lobstr::sxp() reads nothing directly. It asks R through the API: TYPEOF(), ALTREP(), Rf_isObject(), XLENGTH(), ANY_ATTRIB() and R_mapAttrib(), and for the reference count NO_REFERENCES() and MAYBE_SHARED(). The address it prints is the pointer’s value, never dereferenced. It shows less as a result: references as 0, 1 or 2+, and no gp bits, collector state or truelength. Where R 4.5 replaced an accessor, lobstr follows behind #if R_VERSION guards.
  • peek() and a layout copy the memory and decode it against a description of a private structure. That is how it shows the exact reference count and the collector’s size class, which the API does not expose; it is also why a change to the structure in a later R makes it print wrong numbers rather than fail.

Code that runs anywhere but your own console belongs with the second.
